newsitem.title: GERMANY: Strike-hit German confectioners agree pay deals.
newsitem.headline: Strike-hit German confectioners agree pay deals.

text.p: German producers of the confectionery so central to any Christmas celebration here sought on Wednesday to end strikes in the industry by agreeing not to implement an unpopular new law cutting sick pay.
The latest back-downs came during the second week of a strike by confectionery workers that has hit a number of factories around the country, including the Berlin plant of Swiss food group Nestle.

Hanover-based cake-producer Bahlsen said on Wednesday it had agreed that its 3,000 staff should continue to receive sick pay at 100 percent of salary rather than the 80 percent set out by the new law.
Officials of the NGG confectionery-to-restaurant trade union said they were now hopeful of securing deals at other companies as a result of the continuing strikes.
"We are close to break-throughs on other in-house agreements," NGG wage policy chief Gerd Pohl said on German television.

Other firms which have now agreed to keep sick pay entitlements at 100 percent of salary include famous Aachen-based chocolates producer Lindt & Spruengli, which in return has told staff it now expects lower absenteeism.
NGG said it was also optimistic that it could secure an acceptable agreement at the Luebeck marzipan-manufacturer Niederegger.

Confectionery workers are the first in Germany to hold all-out strikes against the deeply unpopular law cutting sick pay brought in this October in by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government as part of an austerity package.

Although strikes on Wednesday involved only some 5,000 workers, the potential impact of the strike in an industry employing just 53,000 staff is great, particularly in the run-up to the Christmas sales season.

The row over sick pay has caused temporary stoppages in other German industries including its huge metal and engineering sector, where protests involving hundreds of thousands of worker have taken place in recent weeks.
Failure by engineering employers and unions to reach agreement on sick pay and other wage issues early next year could result in all-out strikes by workers there next spring.
